intro: Searching for a surveyor usually means you have a property or piece of land you need to understand better, whether you are buying, building, or dealing with a problem that has already surfaced. Surveyors inspect, measure and value property and land, report on condition, advise on building work and help resolve disputes, so the right one depends entirely on what you need to know. Tell us what you are facing and we will introduce you to a suitable UK surveying practice, who will quote you directly.
need_heading: What people searching for a surveyor usually need
need_lead: Most enquiries come from people who need a clear, independent picture of a property before they commit to something.
needs: You are buying a home and want to know what condition it is really in before you exchange contracts.
You have had a building survey done and want advice on what the findings mean and what to do next.
You are planning building work and need someone to advise on the site, the structure or the likely cost.
You are dealing with a dispute with a neighbour or a builder over a boundary, a party wall or the quality of work.
You need a valuation of property or land for a family matter, a lease or another legal reason.
context_heading: Getting the right kind of surveyor matters
context: Surveying covers a wide range of work, and the person who values a house may not be the one who inspects a roof or handles a party wall. Before you enquire, think about which of those jobs you actually need, because it will shape who we introduce you to and what you should ask them.

Many surveyors are members of the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (RICS), and RICS-regulated firms must follow professional standards, hold insurance and offer a complaints process. Chartered surveyors use the letters MRICS or FRICS, and some specialist roles have their own bodies, such as the Faculty of Party Wall Surveyors or the Property Care Association for damp and timber specialists.
tell_heading: What to tell us when you enquire
tell: Describe the property or land, including its age, type and general condition, so we can match the right kind of surveyor.
Say what you need the surveyor for, whether that is a condition report, a valuation, building advice or a dispute.
Explain where the property is, since surveyors work locally and this affects who can help.
Mention any deadline you are working to, such as an exchange date or a court date.
Tell us whether you already have a report or documents that the surveyor should see.
Say whether you are the owner, a buyer or acting for someone else, as this shapes the advice you need.
questions: Which type of survey or report are you recommending for this property, and what does it include?
Are you independent of the sale, and do you have any connection to the seller or the estate agent?
Are you a member of RICS, and what do the letters after your name mean?
What will the report cover, and what will it leave out?
How will you handle anything urgent you find during the inspection?
What is your complaints process if I am unhappy with the work?

faqs.q: Do I need a surveyor if I am buying a home?
faqs.a: A surveyor can give you an independent view of the property's condition before you commit, which is different from a mortgage valuation arranged by your lender. What you need depends on the age and type of the property, so it is worth asking what report suits it.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a valuation and a building survey?
faqs.a: A valuation is an assessment of what the property is worth, often for a lender, while a building survey looks in detail at the condition and structure. Tell the surveyor which one you need so the report matches your purpose.

faqs.q: How do I check a surveyor's credentials?
faqs.a: Many surveyors are members of the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors, and you can check the RICS directory. Chartered surveyors use the letters MRICS or FRICS, and specialist roles may have their own bodies.

faqs.q: Can a surveyor help with a party wall or a boundary dispute?
faqs.a: Yes, surveyors advise on party wall matters and boundary disputes, and some specialise in this work through bodies such as the Faculty of Party Wall Surveyors. Explain the dispute when you enquire so we can introduce someone suited to it.

extra_heading: What a surveyor actually does on a first visit
extra: When you search for a surveyor, you may be picturing a brief walk around the property, but a proper inspection is usually more thorough. The surveyor will examine the structure, the roof, the walls, the floors and the services where visible, and will note any defects, signs of movement or damp. They may use a ladder, a torch or a moisture meter, and they will take photographs as they go.

After the inspection, the surveyor writes a report setting out what they found and what it means for you. The report should be clear about what was inspected and what was not, and it should flag anything that needs further investigation by a specialist. Ask the surveyor to talk you through the findings if anything is unclear, because the report is there to help you make a decision, not to sit unread.

The first visit is also your chance to ask questions about the property and about the surveyor's own qualifications and experience. A good surveyor will be happy to explain their approach and to tell you what they can and cannot cover. This helps you judge whether their report will give you the confidence you need.

extra_faqs.q: Will the surveyor go into the loft or under the floor?
extra_faqs.a: Most surveyors will inspect the loft if it is safely accessible, but they will not move stored items or lift floorboards unless it is part of the agreed scope. Ask beforehand what access they will need and what they will inspect.

extra_faqs.q: Can I be present during the survey?
extra_faqs.a: Some surveyors are happy for you to attend, but others prefer to work alone so they can concentrate. If you do attend, you can ask questions as you go, but remember the written report is the formal record.
